detail 2141 goroutines were created and only 2048 exited during the trace window, leaving 93 goroutines accumulated on top of the 107 that existed at trace start.
suggestion Look for goroutines blocked on channels that are never closed, missing context cancellation, or goroutine-spawning loops without backpressure. Use 'go tool pprof -http=: http://host/debug/pprof/goroutine' to inspect live stacks.
WARN HeapGrowthSpike 145h23m29.6s heap grew by 116.1 MB at 22.8 MB/s over 5.099s (81.4 MB → 197.5 MB)
detail The live heap grew from 81.4 MB to 197.5 MB (+116.1 MB) over 5.099s, a rate of 22.8 MB/s. Rapid heap growth triggers more frequent GC cycles and can force goroutines into GC assist, adding latency on top of STW pauses.
suggestion Check allocation rate with 'go tool pprof -alloc_space'. Look for hot paths that allocate large or many short-lived objects. Consider sync.Pool for frequently allocated types, setting GOMEMLIMIT to cap heap growth, or increasing GOGC to reduce GC frequency.

ERROR GCPauseSpike 145h23m30.81s GC STW pause (GC sweep termination) of 13.832ms exceeds 10ms threshold

WARN ProcessorStarvation 145h23m30.81s P 7 was idle for 13.989ms (threshold: 5ms)
detail Processor 7 sat idle for 13.989ms. During this window it could not execute any goroutines. If goroutines were waiting in the run queue, this represents direct request stall time.
suggestion Check for thread exhaustion: many simultaneous blocking syscalls or CGo calls can starve Ps of OS threads. Verify GOMAXPROCS matches available cores (use automaxprocs in containers). Look for goroutine-per-request patterns without concurrency limits.
